summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1971, the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981 and transvestism in 2011. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence in 1995 and on grounds of gender identity in 2005. Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and other personal characteristics, whether based on fact or assumption; the Act on Equality between Women and Men covers sex and gender identity, and a 2014 amendment extended its protections to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

Legal gender recognition was reformed in 2023: the age limit is 18, down from a proposed 15 with guardian permission, with a 30-day reflection period and a limit of one change per year. Until April 2023 applicants had to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and to hold a mental disorder diagnosis; those requirements are no longer in force.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences, the highest total ever logged, with defamation and assault the most common types. The Police University College reports the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category rising across six reported years, from 72 cases to 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 gives the same headline total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes, a 13% increase since 2023, and identifies sexual orientation and gender identity as recurrent motives, present in 12% of cases. The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime category, so motive is recorded only in police reports; SOGI-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicion rather than as charges.

Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March. Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125 votes to 49 in March; a full statutory ban remained pending.

Marriage equality took effect on 1 March 2017, together with joint adoption. Registered partnerships had been available from 2002 until that date, carrying the rights of married couples except adoption and joint surname, and giving immigration rights to a foreign partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009. A 2018 change to the Maternity Act recognised both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of birth, fixing second-parent registration at birth rather than through adoption. An April 2019 law, passed 122 to 42, gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption. Surrogacy remains illegal for all couples.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. A Seta survey found over 40% of trans respondents entirely unable to access the care they needed, most reporting extended waiting times. In 2020 the Council for Choices in Health Care revised clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25, prioritising psychosocial therapy over medical transition and restricting puberty blockers and hormone treatment; the recommendations are not mandates, so puberty blockers remain available case by case and cross-sex hormones can be considered where the identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria.

Finnish police reported 73 violent attacks and assaults against LGBT people in 2018, a 27% increase on 2017 and the only hate-motive category to rise that year. In November 2019 the Institute of Health and Welfare reported that LGBT children and youth face significantly more bullying, and more physical, psychological and sexual violence, than heterosexual peers, and are more likely to suffer violence at home.
tangentialFactors:
Finland updated its travel advice for transgender citizens travelling to the United States in March 2025, after reports of border difficulties following the US executive order on two genders. The guidance is issued to Finland's own outbound travellers and is not an assessment of risk inside Finland.

Finland is one of six countries examined in Investigate Europe's 'The Cruel Condition' (September 2025) for writing infertility requirements into legal gender recognition law; at least 11,000 people were subjected to such conditions across the six, with Sweden the first to legislate in 1972. The last of the requirements studied was phased out at the end of June 2025.
localsOnly:
Marriage equality reached the statute book through the Tahdon2013 citizens' initiative, which collected more than 162,000 certified signatures, the largest Finnish initiative ever and far above the 50,000 threshold that forces parliamentary consideration; Parliament passed the law in December 2014 by 101 votes to 90. The Constitution allows citizens' initiatives carrying 50,000 valid signatures to be put to Parliament.

Public visibility rests on a 2010 gay rights panel on the state broadcaster Yle TV2, the first public gay demonstration in 1981, and Pride parades in numerous cities, with an estimated 100,000 attending Helsinki Pride in 2018. A gay scene of bars, clubs and cafés operates in Helsinki, and support organisations run nationwide: Seta, founded in 1974, Trasek for trans and intersex rights, and Rainbow Families.

Since December 2023 there is no extra deferral period on blood donation for men who have sex with men.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two sources reporting the 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences differ on the year: the Police University College attributes the figure to 2024, while ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 attributes it to 2025. The discrepancy is unresolved in the material reviewed.

The 1,808 figure is a raw count without a population denominator, and the Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so the total reflects reported suspicion rather than prosecutions or convictions. The 73 attacks recorded in 2018 are likewise a raw count.

Whether the conversion-practices ban endorsed by Parliament in March has since been enacted is not established by the sources reviewed.
